content:
The single biggest risk to fintech right now is AI-powered cyberattacks hitting shared vendor infrastructure. 

Attackers now use AI to automate phishing, deepfakes, and fraud testing, compressing what used to be multi-day attacks into roughly 25 minutes, with nearly half of financial firms already hit by AI-driven attacks in the past year. Because most fintechs plug into the same small set of KYC, payments, and cloud vendors, one breach doesn't stay contained, a single 2025 breach at one vendor, SitusAMC, exposed data from over 100 financial institutions at once.

Why this beats every other risk: Regulation and competition are risks companies can reduce over time by investing more in compliance, capital, or product development. Cyber risk works differently. Attackers need to find just one weakness, while defenders have to protect every entry point and AI has made that challenge even harder.

What makes cyber risk stand out is its ripple effect. A regulatory issue is usually limited to one company or market. But a breach at a shared cloud, payments, or KYC provider can hit hundreds of firms at once, disrupting operations and damaging customer trust across the sector. That's what makes cybersecurity more than just another risk, its impact can spread far beyond a single company.

content:
Life After BBA: Strong Paths That Don't Require an MBA

"Finish your BBA, then do an MBA." For years that was treated as the only sensible route.

But a growing number of BBA graduates are questioning it — and honestly, they're right to.

An MBA still has value. What's changed is that it's no longer the only way to build a serious career. Employers today care more about demonstrable skills than a stacked degree list. LinkedIn's "Jobs on the Rise" reports keep highlighting roles that reward practical ability over pedigree.

So what can you actually do after a BBA without an MBA?
Get certified and specialise — a BBA graduate with a Google Analytics, digital marketing, or financial-modelling certification often becomes job-ready faster than expected
*Enter high-growth functions directly — roles like Digital Marketing Executive, Business Analyst, HR Associate, Sales & Business Development, or Operations Coordinator
*Try entrepreneurship — a BBA (https://lnkd.in/g2J5Q9Qd) already teaches finance, marketing, and operations basics; many graduates launch small ventures or family businesses
Move into fintech, e-commerce, or startups — sectors that hire on skill and hustle, not just an MBA tag
*Pursue niche PG diplomas — shorter, focused programs in analytics, digital marketing, or supply chain

Here's why this matters: a BBA graduate who builds one strong skill — say, running real ad campaigns or analysing business data in Excel and Power BI — can stand out more than someone with a generic MBA and no hands-on ability.

Universities have a role here too. Programs that combine management theory with internships, live projects, and skill certifications prepare students for this reality. Amity University Ranchi, for example, structures its management education around industry exposure, practical learning, and skill development — helping students build career readiness whether or not they choose an MBA later.

So here's my question to students, parents, and hiring managers: In 2026, is an MBA still essential for a strong management career — or are skills and experience becoming the real currency? I'd genuinely like your take.
